concept.name: Canonical concept
concept.definition: The single designated representation of a concept within a controlled vocabulary, to which all synonymous or variant terms (aliases) point. ANSI/NISO Z39.19 calls this the 'preferred term': the term selected to represent a concept in displays and indexing, with non-preferred variants linked to it by equivalence relationships.
concept.intuition: One concept, one official name — every other way of saying it is a pointer back to that name, so nothing is counted or filed twice.
concept.mechanics: Each concept is assigned one preferred term (e.g., 'Moving average convergence divergence') and zero or more non-preferred variants (e.g., 'MACD'); indexing and retrieval systems store the preferred term and resolve variants to it. This keeps counts, citations, and relationships consistent across a corpus.
concept.failure_modes: Fails when a variant is not registered as an alias (the same concept gets indexed twice under different names) or when an overly aggressive canonicalization merges genuinely distinct concepts. Choice of the preferred term can also embed one community's jargon as the default.
concept.misconceptions: Canonical does not mean 'the only correct name in the world' — it is a local convention of one vocabulary; other systems may canonize a different term for the same concept.
concept.example: In this library, 'Relative strength index' is the canonical concept; 'RSI' and 'Wilder's RSI' are aliases that resolve to it, so a document mentioning 'RSI' is indexed under the same entry.

citations.source: ANSI/NISO Z39.19-2005 (R2010), Guidelines for the Construction, Format, and Management of Monolingual Controlled Vocabularies
